title: Drone Show and Fireworks Cap Edison's Fifth Annual Diwali Festival of Lights
excerpt: The Papaianni Park celebration, themed 'Celebrating Diwali in America 250,' paired a diya lighting, dances and food stalls with a Patel Brothers-sponsored aerial finale in a township with one of New Jersey's largest Indian communities.
body:
• Edison's fifth annual Diwali Festival of Lights was scheduled for Saturday, November 7, from 2 to 9 p.m. at Papaianni Park, 100 Municipal Blvd, closing with a drone and fireworks show sponsored by Patel Brothers.
  • The programme, themed "Celebrating Diwali in America 250," included a diya lighting, live music, dance showcases, food and craft vendors, cultural displays and children's activities, with more than 100,000 lights planned.
  • The celebration is free and open to the public; the township encouraged residents to use festival parking and shuttle service, and a rain date of November 14 was set.
  • Edison has hosted the festival since 2022 and has one of New Jersey's largest Asian Indian populations; Diwali itself falls on Sunday, November 8 this year.

Edison's Diwali festivities were set to close on Saturday night with a drone show and fireworks over Papaianni Park, the finale of the township's fifth annual Festival of Lights — a celebration that has grown since 2022 into one of Central Jersey's largest cultural events.

The festival was scheduled for 2 to 9 p.m. on Saturday, November 7, at Papaianni Park, 100 Municipal Blvd, according to MyCentralJersey. The drone and fireworks show, sponsored by Patel Brothers, was planned for after sundown. This year's theme, "Celebrating Diwali in America 250," tied the Hindu festival to the United States' 250th anniversary.

What was on the programme

Alongside the closing display, the festival programme included live musical performances, dance showcases, a diya lighting, food and craft vendors, cultural displays and children's activities. A preview of Diwali celebrations across the US and Canada by the IANS wire, published by NewKerala, described diya lighting, cultural dances, food stalls, free chai and mehndi at Papaianni Park, with more than 100,000 lights planned for the evening.

The celebration is free and open to the public, and residents were encouraged to use festival parking and a shuttle service to travel to and from the event. A rain date of November 14 had been set.

A festival that has grown with the township

Edison has hosted the festival since 2022, when Mayor Sam Joshi, the township's first South Asian mayor, took office. The township has one of New Jersey's largest Asian Indian populations, and the Festival of Lights has grown into one of the state's largest Diwali celebrations, drawing thousands of residents and visitors in recent years.

"Edison's Diwali Festival of Lights reflects the values and spirit that makes Edison so special. This celebration of hope and the triumph of light over darkness has grown to bring tens of thousands of families and friends together."

— Sam Joshi, Mayor of Edison

Part of a wider Diwali weekend

Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8 this year, and the Edison festival was one of several celebrations across New Jersey and the wider region over the weekend. On Oak Tree Road in nearby Iselin, a gathering featured a Ramlila performance by Pandit Satya Narayan Charka and 40 classically trained artists, with music and cultural performances, according to the IANS report. Jersey City also hosted "Diwali Together 2026" at Exchange Place on Saturday, from noon to 7 p.m.

Diwali, derived from the Sanskrit "Deepavali," meaning "row of lights," is observed by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists. Devotees light lamps outside their homes during the festival, marking the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil.

Township officials also used the week to remind residents to celebrate safely under New Jersey's fireworks laws: since 2017 the state has allowed certain ground-based fireworks such as handheld sparklers, smoke devices and party poppers, while aerial fireworks, including bottle rockets, firecrackers and Roman candles, remain prohibited.
